cv.alt: Tolgee supplying content to a Next.js page, which also renders a PDF built by Chromium, publishes contact messages to Kafka for the shared notifications service to deliver, and sends visitors' questions with the CV to the Claude API for answers that cite it.
cv.caption: The same content renders twice: an editorial page for a person, and a single-column document for a parser. Building the PDF at compile time is what keeps its text real rather than a picture of text. A third path reads the same content again: a question and the whole CV go to Claude, and only an answer that cites the CV comes back.

designSystem.alt: The design system in three layers — tokens, then components that reference only tokens, then per-product themes — pinned as a tagged dependency in each consumer.
designSystem.caption: Themes override colour and nothing else. Shape, type scale and spacing stay on shared tokens, so a full reskin touches no component file.

gpool.alt: The gpool request path: a Next.js front end calling a NestJS API backed by Postgres, with the API publishing email intent to Kafka for the shared notifications service to deliver.
gpool.caption: The API publishes an email intent and moves on. Delivery, idempotency and dead-lettering belong to a service that already does them, so joining a pool never waits on an SMTP call.

kini.alt: kini, and the practices extracted from it — the translation workflow, release automation and compose layout — carried into the repositories that followed.
kini.caption: Kept as its own repository rather than folded into gpool, so the rewrite could change its mind about the architecture without rewriting history.

notifications.alt: A delivery pipeline reading a versioned topic through a consumer, idempotency claims and locale-resolved templates to a sent email, with malformed payloads branching off to a dead-letter record.
notifications.caption: Invalid payloads fail as non-retryable and land in a durable record. Retrying a malformed message forever is a worse outcome than losing it loudly.

platformOps.alt: The products attached to one shared Docker network, which fronts three families of service: secrets and translations, events, and observability.
platformOps.caption: Seven of the eleven services are observability. That ratio is deliberate: the expensive part of running several small services is not running them, it is being able to see them.

sity.alt: A road plan feeding a network builder that produces both the directed lane graph and the drawn scene, with the verification reading the graph back through the page.
sity.caption: Roads are drawn from the graph rather than the graph fitted to the drawing, so a vehicle on lane data is on the asphalt.

cv.approach: One source of content, rendered twice. The page is an editorial layout with a case study behind each project; the same data renders a separate single-column document that headless Chromium turns into a PDF during the build, so the parsed version keeps real selectable text rather than a picture of it. The same source also answers questions: a box in the header sends the question together with the whole CV to Claude, and an answer only reaches the reader if it cites the parts of the CV it came from, each one a link back into the page.
decisions: The PDF is generated at build time rather than in the browser. Client-side html-to-PDF libraries rasterise the page, destroying the selectable text the entire ATS layout exists to produce.

Nothing it publishes carries a way to reach a person directly. The contact form reaches the same inbox through a secret held in OpenBao, so no address appears in the page, the PDF or the structured data. The answer box inherits the rule: a reply containing anything shaped like an address, a phone number or a profile link is replaced before it is sent.
The contact endpoint sends RFC 9457 problem details like the four APIs, so one error shape covers the whole estate rather than four.

An answer is grounded by the citations the API returns, not by an instruction to stay on topic. One that cites nothing is replaced with a refusal before it leaves the server, which is why answers are checked whole rather than streamed.

Spend is capped in three places that fail differently: a per-visitor rate limit in memory, a monthly budget written to a volume so a restart cannot reset it, and a spending limit on the API workspace that holds even if both of those are lost. The API key itself is optional, so a deploy without it still serves the CV and simply hides the box.

Every question is logged with its outcome, citations, tokens and cost, and never with the address it came from, so what was asked cannot be joined back to who asked it. The questions the CV fails to answer are the most useful thing the box produces.

pieces.text: Every word lives in Tolgee under a cv.* namespace — the case studies, the section names and the PDF headings included. What stays in code is only what reads identically in every language: ids, ordering and technology names.
pieces.title: Content

pieces.text: Next.js in standalone output, with the locale resolved on the server from a cookie, then Accept-Language, then the default, so the tab title and the search snippet follow the selected language rather than lagging a request behind it.
pieces.title: The page

pieces.text: A separate print document built for extraction — one column, conventional headings, no icons, contact details in plain text — rendered by Chromium during the Docker build, which fails if the file cannot be produced.
pieces.title: The PDF

pieces.text: A route handler sends the question with the CV as one document split into content blocks — one per role, skill group and part of a case study — with citations switched on. Each citation comes back as a block index that maps straight to a section or a case-study tab, so every source is a link rather than a quote. The CV sits in a cached prefix, so the later questions of a visit reread it at a tenth of the price.
pieces.title: The answer box

pieces.text: Every request is a trace. A page render, the question sent to Claude with the tokens and the cost it came back with, the flags read on the way, and the message handed to the broker are one timeline in the platform's store rather than four guesses. Every line it writes carries the trace it was written inside, so a failure found in the logs opens the request that caused it, and a question refused or cut short is found without reading any of them. The traffic that would drown it — the container health check, the metrics scrape, the browser beacons, the static files — is dropped before it is ever recorded.
pieces.title: What it reports

pieces.text: What it depends on, it reports on. Tolgee, Unleash and the broker each say whether they answered the last time they were asked, and the broker is asked every fifteen seconds rather than waiting for the next visitor's message. None of them can take the page down: a failure reads as degraded, the page renders from the committed copy with the declared flag defaults, and the alert names the part that is missing. Every request the three endpoints serve is counted and timed, and a slow one carries the id of its own trace.
pieces.title: Honest health

pieces.text: The browser reports what a visit actually felt like: the Core Web Vitals once per page view under their current definitions, with the element behind any poor one, and every script error with the source line that threw it — mapped back through the build's source maps, with anything personal masked out of the message. A page load carries the id of the trace that rendered it, so a slow visit opens its own server side. The funnel is counted as well — questions answered or failed, messages sent, the PDF downloaded, case studies opened — and each series names the release that served it. The content security policy still only reports: every violation is counted and logged by directive before anything is enforced, and each page carries a fresh nonce, so the site's own scripts pass and only a foreign one is reported.
pieces.title: What visitors see

automation: Dependabot opens grouped pull requests once a week and waits seven days before proposing a newly published version. A compromised release is usually caught and yanked within days, and nothing here is urgent enough to be worth installing first. Base-image majors are never proposed: a new Node major changes the runtime, so it lands on purpose, together with the version pin and the engines range.

Auto-merge is enabled the moment a non-draft pull request opens, but only when its owner or Dependabot opened it from inside the repository, and only collaborators can open pull requests at all. Branch protection does the rest: green checks merge, red ones sit. Dependabot majors are the one exclusion, because a major is a change to read rather than a number to bump.
CodeQL, dependency review and Semgrep run on every pull request, and the SBOM is kept as an artefact of each one rather than only of a release.

The observability code is copied in from the platform repository rather than installed from a registry, so a pin beside it records the digest of the kit it was copied from. An edit to a copy fails the pull request without going to the network, so that check cannot be flaky; the kit having moved on is only reported there, because every product is behind for the days between a kit change and someone doing the rounds, and a weekly scheduled run is what eventually fails for it. A deliberate fork is declared in the pin with its reason, and a declaration that stops matching what is on disk fails as well.
The PDF is rendered by headless Chromium inside the Docker build, which fails if the file cannot be produced. A deploy cannot ship a page and a stale PDF that disagree with each other.

The deploy bundle is the repository at the released commit, so the host runs the deploy script belonging to the release it is deploying. Rolling back to an older tag restores that release's deploy logic with it, rather than running today's script against last month's compose file.

A push to main touching the message files, the Tolgee config or the production environment promotes the committed copy into the production Tolgee project, so wording ships without a release. The push is retried, and a promotion that still fails opens one labelled issue and comments on it rather than leaving a red mark nobody reads. Nothing the running site measures can catch it: a failed promotion leaves Tolgee answering with yesterday's wording, so every render still counts as translated.

The translation pull and the running site ask Tolgee for the same export shape and refuse anything else. One that arrives with dotted keys, or with no messages in it at all, is turned away at both ends: the site falls back to the committed copy, and the pull writes nothing at all. Tolgee is still reported up, because it answered — restarting it would only serve the same body again — so an unusable export is raised from the logs instead, as a ticket that waits an hour rather than a page nobody can act on. A bad export costs sixty seconds of stale wording rather than a commit that rewrites every message file.

Local development has two modes over one set of containers. `local:up` runs the production image, so what is being checked is what ships; `local:dev` builds a dev stage instead and runs `next dev` under `docker compose watch`, which copies changed files into the running container rather than rebuilding it. The rebuild it skips includes the Chromium PDF render, the slowest step in the image.

stages.text: Husky runs gitleaks over the staged diff, then the vendored observability code against the kit digest this repository pinned, then lint, typecheck, the unit suite and build, so a workspace that does not compile or pass its tests never becomes a branch. commitlint holds the message to Conventional Commits — release-please reads those later to decide the version — and a pre-push hook refuses to push to main at all.
stages.title: Before the commit

stages.text: Seven jobs in parallel: quality (format, the vendored kit against its pin, lint, typecheck, unit tests and build), a full-repository secret scan, a Docker smoke that boots the production image and probes it, including that the question endpoint stays closed without a key and that the unprivileged user can write the directory holding the monthly budget, Playwright asserting WCAG 2.1 AA and Core Web Vitals budgets in a real browser, the three compose manifests rendered against a placeholder environment, licences with a production-only audit alongside an SBOM and Trivy, and Semgrep. A run superseded by a newer commit is cancelled rather than left holding a runner.
stages.title: The pull request

stages.text: release-please keeps a release pull request open against main, deriving the next version and the changelog from the conventional commits since the last tag. Merging it tags and publishes the release, so cutting one is a merge rather than a command somebody runs on a laptop.
stages.title: The release

stages.text: A published release builds the image, pushes it to ECR, scans the pushed image with Trivy before anything signs it — a signature over an unscanned image says it was built here, not that it is fit to run — and has cosign sign it keylessly by digest, with SLSA provenance and an SPDX SBOM attached — by digest, because a tag can be repointed after signing. The compose bundle goes to S3 and SSM runs the deploy script on the EC2 host, so no runner ever holds an SSH key. A smoke job then probes the public health endpoint, so a deploy that reports success but serves nothing fails here rather than in a browser.
stages.title: The deploy

cv.problem: A CV is read by two audiences that want opposite things. A person wants something worth looking at; an applicant tracking system wants one column of plain text under conventional headings. Serving either one well usually breaks the other. And a reader who arrives with one specific question still has to read all of it to find the answer.
cv.tagline: This site: a CV that renders itself twice, once for a person and once for a parser.

design-system.approach: Components are plain React styled only through CSS custom properties, with no Tailwind, no CSS-in-JS and no build step. Any of the three can import them as-is, and each supplies its own theme file rather than editing component source.
decisions: Themes override colour only. Shape, type scale and spacing stay on shared base tokens, so every product renders identical geometry and differs solely in paint.
Published as a tagged dependency rather than vendored into each consumer: a change arrives as a version bump in a reviewable pull request, and every product can be checked to be on the same tag.

pieces.text: Colour, typography, spacing, radius, shadow and motion as oklch-based custom properties, with one neutral default theme.
pieces.title: Tokens

pieces.text: Primitives grouped by concern — core, forms, feedback, data-display, navigation, overlay, icons — each referencing tokens only, never a literal colour.
pieces.title: Components

pieces.text: One file per product overriding colour tokens. A full reskin touches zero component files.
pieces.title: Themes

automation: The manifest is generated, and CI fails when the committed one differs from a fresh run. A hand-edited manifest is how a component quietly disappears from the list every consumer reads.

Every component in the manifest is mounted and run through axe in the test run, and the specimen pages are checked in a real browser, so a component that no longer renders — or a token pairing that fails contrast — fails here rather than in whichever product upgrades first.
Dependabot on npm and the Actions; the components themselves have no runtime dependencies to update.
A secret scan and Semgrep on every pull request, the same two gates as everywhere else — a repository with no build is not a repository with no risk.

stages.text: No build, no bundle and nothing for a consumer to install — this is components, tokens and guidelines that other repositories vendor. So CI checks the things that can actually go wrong: a leaked secret, a manifest that no longer matches what is on disk, and a component or a token pairing that fails accessibility. The manifest has to be regenerated rather than hand-edited, every component listed in it is mounted and run through axe, the JSON files are parsed, and Playwright opens every specimen page in Chromium to check WCAG A and AA — colour contrast included, which only exists where layout and paint do.
stages.title: The pull request

stages.text: release-please cuts a version from the conventional commits. That tag is the entire distribution: products depend on the repository at a pinned tag, so there is no registry publish to fail and no unpublished version to chase.
stages.title: The release

stages.text: A design system release deploys nothing by itself. Each product picks it up when its own Dependabot bumps the pinned tag, and it then ships through that product's pipeline — which is why a component change reaches each product on that product's schedule rather than all at once.
stages.title: The upgrade

design-system.problem: Three products had drifted into three styling technologies — plain CSS classes, Tailwind utilities and CVA variants — and no shared visual language. Picking one framework would have meant rewriting two applications.
design-system.tagline: A technology-agnostic token and component library three products share without agreeing on a CSS framework.

gpool.approach: One monorepo with a NestJS API and a Next.js web app, both joining a shared platform rather than owning their own infrastructure. Secrets, translations, the event broker and observability all come from platform-ops; gpool ships only the two containers that are actually its own.
decisions: Secrets are fetched at boot by a wrapper process, never baked into an image or committed to an env file, so a leaked app token exposes one kv path rather than the whole store.
Email is an event, not a call. The API publishes to a topic and a shared service owns delivery, idempotency and dead-lettering.
CI regenerates the web API contract from the running API and fails on drift, so client and server cannot disagree silently.

Errors are RFC 9457 problem details with a translatable code, and every route declares its status code — which is how it came out that Nest was answering 201 to POSTs the generated client documented as 200.

Which copy a render served is counted, not assumed. A page that falls back to the committed translations still renders, so a health check reads it as up — which is how a language once stayed stale for months behind a green signal.

pieces.text: NestJS monolith covering auth and pools. It owns the Google OAuth exchange and issues the session itself, so the client secret lives in one service rather than two. Runs database migrations on startup, exposes an OpenAPI spec, and publishes email intent as Kafka events rather than sending mail itself.
pieces.title: API

pieces.text: Next.js App Router in standalone output, talking to the API directly with a session cookie rather than proxying every call to sign its own headers. Translations are fetched from Tolgee per request behind a sixty-second cache and merged over the copy committed in the repository, so wording ships without a release and an unreachable Tolgee falls back to the committed words; the container starts under a wrapper that fetches its secrets from OpenBao and refuses to boot without the keys it declares. It takes its own visitors' Core Web Vitals, script errors and content security reports, so what a visit felt like is measured where the page is served.
pieces.title: Web

pieces.text: Images build to ECR on release, a bundle lands in S3, and SSM drives a compose deploy on the shared EC2 host. CI gates on lint, typecheck, coverage, a compose integration smoke, gitleaks, SBOM and a Trivy scan.
pieces.title: Delivery

automation: Translations promote themselves. A push to main touching the message files, the Tolgee config or the production env promotes the copy to the production Tolgee project, so wording ships without a release. The push is retried, and a promotion that still fails opens one labelled issue and comments on it, so stale wording is visible as a task rather than a red mark nobody reads.

Dependabot watches four ecosystems — npm, both Dockerfiles and the Actions themselves — grouped weekly, with patch and minor merging on green and majors left for a person. Base-image majors are not proposed at all, so the Node runtime only moves on purpose.
The public endpoints are probed every five minutes from outside the estate by platform-ops, which opens an issue when one stops answering.
CodeQL, dependency review and Semgrep on every pull request; Trivy and the SBOM again at deploy, against the image that is actually shipping rather than the one CI happened to build.

Both applications carry the observability code copied in from the platform repository, and a pin beside them records the digest of the kit those copies came from. An edit to a copy fails the pull request without going to the network; the kit having moved on is only reported there and fails a weekly scheduled run instead, because every product is behind for the days between a kit change and someone doing the rounds. The API's copies of the kit's tests are renamed for the test runner that collects them, and the pin declares that renaming rather than leaving six files outside the comparison.

Local development has two modes over one set of containers. `local:up` runs the production images; `local:dev` builds a dev stage of each and runs `nest start --watch` and `next dev` under `docker compose watch`, so an edit reaches the running container as a file sync instead of an image rebuild. Dependency manifests still trigger a rebuild, because a lockfile change cannot be copied in.

The translation pull merges rather than replaces. Starting the local stack syncs with Tolgee, and a Tolgee that is empty or behind used to delete committed copy it did not know about; wording that has not been pushed yet now survives the sync.

stages.text: The same three hooks every repository here carries: gitleaks over the staged diff followed by the vendored observability code against the kit digest this repository pinned, then lint, typecheck, build and both unit suites; commitlint on the message; and a pre-push hook that refuses main. CI sets HUSKY=0 so the hooks never run a second time on a runner that is already running them as jobs.
stages.title: Before the commit

stages.text: Five jobs: quality — compose manifests rendered, the vendored kit against its pin, lint, typecheck, build, API unit tests with coverage uploaded and the web suite — a secret scan, an integration smoke that stands the whole stack up under Compose and then opens a real browser on it — the sign-in page rendered, axe against WCAG A and AA, Core Web Vitals budgets, and the sign-in and pools pages checked against their own content security policy — before a k6 load smoke, security and supply chain, and Semgrep.

stages.text: release-please derives the version and the changelog from the conventional commits on main, and publishes the tag when its pull request is merged.
stages.title: The release

stages.text: Both images are built, Trivy-scanned before they leave the runner, then signed with cosign and given SLSA provenance and an SBOM attestation, all bound to the digest. S3 carries the bundle, SSM applies it on the host, and a post-deploy smoke hits the public health endpoint — the only check that can fail after production has already changed.

gpool.problem: A prediction pool needs more than a spreadsheet: authentication, scoring that settles on a schedule, notifications, and a record of why anyone holds the points they do. Every one of those is a service, and standing them up per project does not scale.
gpool.tagline: A real-time football pool platform: private pools, live scoring, and an auditable trail of every point.

kini.approach: A NestJS API and Next.js client in one monorepo, with monitoring wired in locally. Much of what it worked out — the compose layout, the Tolgee translation flow, the release and deploy workflows — became the template the later projects started from.
decisions: Kept as its own repository rather than folded into gpool, so the rewrite could change its mind about the architecture without rewriting history.

Errors are RFC 9457 problem details with a translatable code, and resources are plural and nested: a match now lives under the pool that owns it, and the pool in the path is checked rather than decorative.

pieces.text: NestJS backend and Next.js client, sharing a compose stack and a single set of CI workflows.

pieces.text: The translation workflow, the commit and release automation, and the local-first compose layout were all extracted and reused rather than rebuilt.
pieces.title: What carried forward

automation: A proof of concept runs the same pipeline as production. The point of owning the template is that a new idea starts with signed images, a smoke test and a changelog rather than earning them later, when retrofitting is exactly what nobody has time for.
Dependabot across npm, both Dockerfiles and the Actions, grouped weekly, with patch and minor merging on green. Base-image majors are not proposed, so the Node runtime only moves on purpose.
CodeQL, dependency review and Semgrep on every pull request.

The observability code in both applications is copied in from the platform repository, and a pin beside it records the digest of the kit it came from. An edit to a copy fails the pull request without going to the network, so that check cannot be flaky; the kit having moved on is only reported there and fails a weekly scheduled run instead, because every product is behind for the days between a kit change and someone doing the rounds.

Local development has two modes over one set of containers. `local:up` runs the production images; `local:dev` builds a dev stage of each and runs `nest start --watch` and `next dev` under `docker compose watch`, so an edit reaches the running container as a file sync instead of an image rebuild. Dependency manifests still trigger a rebuild, because a lockfile change cannot be copied in.

The translation pull merges the export into the committed message files instead of replacing them, so a local sync against an empty Tolgee cannot delete wording nobody has pushed yet — the same guard cv and gpool run.

Translations promote themselves here too. A push to main touching the message files promotes the committed copy into the production Tolgee project, and a promotion that fails after its retries opens one labelled issue instead of going unnoticed — a failed promotion leaves Tolgee answering with yesterday's wording, so nothing the running site measures can catch it.

kini.problem: The original attempt at a pool platform: teams, invitations, and scoring, built before there was any shared infrastructure to lean on.
kini.tagline: The first football pool platform, and the one that taught me what gpool needed to be.

notifications.approach: One consumer owns delivery for all of them. Producers publish an intent event and stop caring; the service validates the contract, renders a localised template, sends it, and keeps a durable record of every attempt.
decisions: Invalid payloads fail as non-retryable and go to a durable dead-letter record, because retrying a malformed message forever is a worse outcome than losing it loudly.
A versioned topic name, so a contract change is a new topic rather than a silent break for every producer.
Errors are RFC 9457 problem details like every other service, even though this one serves nothing but health and metrics — the 404s and 500s it does emit are the ones nobody writes a client for.

When the dead-letter write itself fails, the record is held rather than dropped: the offset stays uncommitted and that partition stops, because an email lost in silence is worse than a queue that visibly waits. The consumer names the record it is stuck on and how many times it has failed.

pieces.text: Reads a versioned topic under a stable consumer group and validates every event against an explicit contract, rejecting malformed payloads as non-retryable rather than looping on them.
pieces.title: Consumer

pieces.text: Atomic idempotency claims stop duplicate sends, and processing leases let a crashed worker’s in-flight messages be picked up rather than stranded.
pieces.title: Delivery

pieces.text: Handlebars templates keyed by source application and template id, resolved per locale, with data escaped on render so sender-controlled content cannot inject markup.
pieces.title: Templates

pieces.text: Every email carries the trace of whatever asked for it. The message cv or gpool published continues into the claim on the database, the template render and the SMTP conversation, so a delivery that took nine seconds reads as four spans rather than being inferred from three log lines. No span carries an address: the request id finds the row, and the row has the recipient.
pieces.title: The trail

pieces.text: The objective is about email, not requests: 99% of emails sent within two minutes of being asked for, with alerts when that budget burns. The SMTP relay counts as a dependency like the database — when it rejects the login or stops answering, health reports it down and pages, and the consumer pauses and retries rather than dead-lettering, so the emails wait in the topic and go out when the relay is back. Dead letters are for messages that can never succeed.
pieces.title: Holding mail through an outage

automation: Every deploy reads the service's own health before it is called done — Postgres, the consumer group and the relay — from the host, because this service has no public route. A release that comes back with a rejected SMTP login fails the workflow instead of dead-lettering email quietly.
Compose manifests are rendered in CI, so a file that no longer parses fails on the pull request rather than on the host, halfway through a deploy.
The integration job dumps the container logs when it fails. A red run without them only tells you to reproduce it locally, which is the slowest possible way to learn what the broker did.
Dependabot on npm, the Dockerfile and the Actions, weekly and grouped; patch and minor merge on green. Base-image majors are not proposed, so the Node runtime only moves on purpose.
CodeQL, dependency review and Semgrep on every pull request.

Local development has two modes over one container. `local:up` runs the production image; `local:dev` builds a dev stage and runs `nest start --watch` under `docker compose watch`, so an edit to the worker reaches it as a file sync instead of an image rebuild. Dependency manifests still trigger a rebuild, because a lockfile change cannot be copied in.

stages.text: gitleaks over the staged diff, then lint, typecheck and build; commitlint on the message; and a pre-push hook that refuses main.
stages.title: Before the commit

stages.text: Six jobs, one of which is the one that matters: the service runs against a real Kafka, a real PostgreSQL and an SMTP sink. Idempotency and dead-lettering are claims about what a broker does under redelivery, and a mocked broker will agree with whatever the code already believes.
stages.title: The pull request

stages.text: release-please, with the version mirrored into the API package and its lockfile entry so the artefact and the tag cannot drift apart.
stages.title: The release

stages.text: The API image is built and pushed, scanned with Trivy before signing, signed with cosign by digest with SLSA provenance and an SPDX SBOM attached, bundled to S3 and applied on the host through SSM, then smoke-tested against the public health endpoint.
stages.title: The deploy

notifications.problem: Every product eventually needs to send mail, and every product that does it inline reinvents retries, deduplication and the question of what happened to a message that never arrived.
notifications.tagline: A Kafka-backed email service the other products delegate delivery to, with idempotency and crash recovery built in.

platform-ops.approach: One ops stack, one external Docker network, and a rule that applications own only their own containers. An app declares which secret path it reads and which topics it uses; everything underneath is shared and versioned in one place.
decisions: Per-application OpenBao policies scoped to exactly one kv path, so an app token is useless against any other app.
The same compose manifests describe local and production, so a local reproduction is a real reproduction.

The whole estate runs on one host by design, which leaves cost a single lever: stop it. A scheduled window and a manual switch turn production off for the hours nobody uses it, and everything comes back on its own from the disk.

One HTTP contract for five services: RFC 9457 problem details carrying a translatable code, plural nested resources, explicit status codes per verb, and a URL version only where a separately deployed service is the caller.

pieces.text: One external Docker network, platform_ops_shared. An application joins it, resolves every shared service by container alias, and needs to know nothing else about the topology. There is no service mesh and no discovery layer — joining the network is the whole contract, which is why every repository creates it before anything else starts.
pieces.title: The integration seam

pieces.text: OpenBao holds every application secret behind a policy scoped to exactly one kv path, and a boot wrapper fetches them and refuses to start a container missing a key it declared. It unseals itself from a KMS key nothing else on the host can reach, so a reboot no longer leaves production without secrets. Tolgee holds the copy, which applications pull as a snapshot at build time and merge live at request time. Unleash holds the switches behind its own domain on the shared ingress, reached by applications over the internal network: an application declares which flags it has and what they default to, and the server supplies values, so losing it degrades to those defaults rather than to an outage.
pieces.title: Secrets, translations and flags

pieces.text: Redpanda speaks the Kafka API without a JVM or ZooKeeper, carrying versioned topics such as notification.email.requested.v1 — how an application hands off an email instead of sending one itself. A console for browsing topics, consumer groups and messages runs locally only; production has no reason to expose it.
pieces.title: Events

pieces.text: Traces are pushed by the application to an OTel collector and stored in Tempo, which keeps them for thirty days and turns every span into metrics with an exemplar attached — which is how a page render, counted by no route, gets a latency objective of its own. Metrics are scraped the other way round — Prometheus reaches into each application on a schedule, and routes whatever fires to Alertmanager. Logs need no participation at all: Alloy tails them off the host into Loki, so applications only ever write to stdout. Grafana reads all three and is the one place anyone actually looks. Every alert carries the environment that raised it, so production is never mistaken for a laptop. A fix on that first path changed what a page render looks like: the kit emits one server span per Next request instead of three, because the incoming HTTP span duplicated Next's own and the middleware pass added a second with no route in its name, and anything aggregating by span kind was counting a page view three times. The pass that hands the request on is held rather than dropped, and discarded only once the request it handed to ends; a pass nothing supersedes is kept. So a 404, which hands on to nothing, still keeps the one span that explains it. The trade is deliberate: without that incoming span a Next request is no longer a single trace, which is the price of counting a page view once.
pieces.title: Three signals, three paths

pieces.text: Commit hooks that scan for secrets, parse every workflow, render every compose file and check Terraform formatting before anything reaches CI.
pieces.title: Guardrails

pieces.text: Grafana 13 provisions every dashboard in five folders — the estate, each service, what visitors experience, the platform itself, and what people do and what it costs — and none is edited by hand: a TypeScript generator writes them, and a test fails when the committed JSON differs from its output or a panel queries a metric nothing exports. Every graph marks deploys from the release each service reports, counting only a version not seen in the three days before, so a host switched off overnight is not a deploy every morning. Every alert names its dashboard, and the email opens it on the service and the hours around the alert, two clicks from the failing trace.
pieces.title: Dashboards as code

automation: Every weekday at 10:15 the host exports to S3 each day of logs that is not archived yet, one gzipped file per day and service with a manifest recording the line counts. Loki deletes at thirty days and the export runs ahead of it, catching up any day it missed, so a weekend with the machine switched off costs nothing. Glacier takes the files after a month and deletes them after a year, which puts a year of logs in the region of a few cents.

Every weekday at 10:45 the host removes the Docker images that no container uses and that were built more than a week ago. Every release leaves its previous image behind, and for months nothing removed them, until the disk stood at 94% with 54 GB of images nothing ran. A week is long enough that rolling back to anything recent still needs no pull.

An uptime probe runs every five minutes on GitHub's infrastructure and checks the public health endpoints from outside. Prometheus runs on the same host as the things it watches, so it cannot report its own death — and the silence looks exactly like everything being fine.
The probe opens a GitHub issue rather than sending mail. An issue deduplicates, carries a state, and does not depend on the SMTP relay, which is itself one of the things that could be broken.
Scheduled runs are best effort by design: GitHub delays them under load and skips them outright on a busy account, so this is roughly every five minutes and never a heartbeat.

One prettier configuration and one ignore body across the eight repositories, with a format gate that covers application source rather than workflows and documentation alone. Everything generated is named in that shared ignore — build output, the Next-written next-env.d.ts, the OpenAPI client CI diffs against the running API, the design-system manifest compared byte for byte — because prettier reads that file and not .gitignore.

Every unit suite in the estate carries a coverage floor set at what it reaches today, so a change that deletes a tested path fails the job instead of quietly lowering the number. The figures differ widely by repository — the low twenties in the gpool API, the mid nineties in the sity lane graph — because they are measurements rather than targets. The Rust workspace has one too, through cargo llvm-cov rather than vitest, and it is the only lane that does not drift: three separate runs reported the same 3176 of 11424 lines to the fourth decimal.

The observability kit is vendored into every product rather than published, because a private registry would put a token in every CI run and a build secret in every image for a dozen files. What that costs is drift, so the copies are checked instead of trusted. A manifest carries a hash per file and a digest over all of them: an edited or missing copy fails offline and blocks the pull request that made it, and a deviation has to be declared with a reason, so one that has stopped being needed fails too. Being behind the kit is the other half and cannot be seen without the network, and a network failure must never redden an unrelated pull request, so it is reported by default and only fails in the strict mode a weekly run would use. The kit is held to its own manifest here today; the products adopt the check, and that weekly run with it, next.

The standard is a script rather than a document: it reads all eight repositories from one root and checks what a terminal can check — hooks armed by npm install, one Node pin agreeing with the engines range and with the images, one prettier configuration, every README opening on the same sections in the same order, the shared scripts byte for byte. A weekly run clones each repository at main, runs it, and keeps one labelled issue open while anything fails, closing it when nothing does. The first honest run found the verifier itself: started from a worktree it resolved a root holding no repositories, skipped every section and reported that all checks passed. The gates it covers had the same shape — a licence check over an empty dependency tree, a syntax check matching no scripts — so each now fails when it inspects nothing rather than issuing a clean bill of health.
Dependabot on npm and the Actions, weekly and grouped, with patch and minor merging on green.

A Power workflow stops and starts the single production host on demand, and two EventBridge Scheduler rules do the same on a fixed daily window. Off means a stopped machine, not a torn-down one: every database, the secret store and the certificates stay on its volume, and the uptime probe reads the host's state first, so a deliberate stop is a silence it expects.

stages.text: Two hooks rather than three: a pre-commit that scans and checks, and a pre-push that refuses main. Commit messages are held to Conventional Commits by a workflow instead of a local hook, since much of what lands here arrives as a dependency bump rather than as somebody typing a message.
stages.title: Before the commit

stages.text: Shared infrastructure is mostly not application code, so the checks are not application checks: formatting, a syntax check of every shell script, workflow and compose linting, terraform validate against both stacks, the observability kit and the dashboard generator typechecked and tested, and the deploy script's env-file helpers under bats. The generator's tests fail when a committed dashboard is not what it writes, or when a panel queries a metric nothing exports. A second check reads the alert wiring rather than the dashboards: that every alert has a runbook row, that an inhibit rule compares only labels the alert actually carries, and that a container given a memory limit has told its runtime about it. Each is escapable only by declaring the exception with its reason, so an exception that has stopped being needed fails too. A secret scan and Semgrep alongside them.
stages.title: The pull request

stages.text: release-please in simple mode. There is no package to version here — only a tag and a changelog that record what the shared platform now is, which is what the products pin themselves against.
stages.title: The release

stages.text: A published release, or a manual dispatch, packages the tracked files into a bundle, uploads it to S3 and has SSM apply it on the host. The shared stack deploys down exactly the same path as the products sitting on it, which is how that path stays trustworthy: everything exercises it. It restarts the secret store only when that store's own config changed — a mount path carrying the release name used to recreate it on every release. Containers of services a release no longer defines are removed, so retiring one is a deletion in the compose file rather than a command typed on the host.
stages.title: The deploy

platform-ops.problem: Five applications each needed secret storage, translations, an event broker and observability. Duplicating that per repository means five OpenBao instances to unseal and five ways to be inconsistent.
platform-ops.tagline: The shared operations stack every other project attaches to instead of rebuilding.

sity.approach: One plan describes every road as nodes and typed segments. From it the scene builds the geometry it renders and the directed lane graph that vehicles will follow, so the drawing and the data cannot disagree. The terrain follows the roads and the streams (cuttings, embankments, tunnel portals and culverts come from the same centrelines, and the ground is clamped below every paved surface), every dead end finishes at a destination whose parking bays are exported for the simulation, and the city grows from the streets: lots are cut along each frontage and filled with instanced buildings whose facades come from a shader.
decisions: Roads are drawn from the graph rather than the graph fitted to the drawing. A road rendered from the same sampled centreline as its lanes means a vehicle on lane data is on the asphalt, with no second source of truth to reconcile.

Everything repeated is instanced and everything else is merged per material, which keeps the whole 13 km² site under 600 draw calls and 4.6 million triangles with post-processing on. The facade grid is computed in the shader from the instance box, so building variety costs attributes, not geometry.

pieces.text: A ring highway with a tunnel, a cable-stayed bridge and viaducts; a diamond, a dumbbell, a half-diamond, a trumpet and a cloverleaf, plus a road under the viaduct; two motorways that leave the map at its edges: one south with a lane drop, a rest area on its own ramps and a rural overpass, one west through a mountain tunnel with a diamond, a services area and free-flow toll gantries; a downtown grid with bus lanes, left-turn pockets and cycle tracks on the arterials, collectors, a one-way pair, a school zone, roundabouts, a curved riverside collector and two river bridges; a railway with a gated level crossing and a station forecourt, a village loop, a hospital drive and farm lanes; in the mountains a forest road, a valley road to a pass and a switchback col road to an alpine village; and beyond the pass, rural roads through a dense pine forest with a hamlet and a lake and across farmland with a farm village, where brooks are crossed by culverts and small bridges. Each road carries its class rules for lanes, medians, sidewalks and speed, and every dead end is a car park, forecourt, yard or viewpoint.
pieces.title: Road plan

pieces.text: Every lane is a directed polyline with successors, predecessors and neighbours. Junction connectors are generated per allowed turn, roundabouts as circulating arcs, ramps as diverges and merges. Dijkstra routing, path enumeration and invariant checks live on the same graph.
pieces.title: Lane graph

pieces.text: Districts decide what a lot becomes: towers on podiums downtown, brick and plaster blocks, houses with gardens, chalets on the mountain, sheds by the port, hotels on the coast. Facades are a shader over per-instance attributes, so a few thousand buildings cost a handful of draw calls. Forests, street trees, parks, a plaza, an arena, a multi-storey car park, a school, churches, a station, a hospital, hedged fields and a generated farmland grid with farmyards, a manor, a sawmill, a farmers' co-op, a wind farm, a golf course, a campsite, two motorway services, a chairlift, a container terminal, an amusement pier and a beach with its promenade fill the rest, with parked cars in every bay and bus stops on the main streets. A footprint audit keeps buildings off pavements and off each other.
pieces.title: City

pieces.text: Vitest covers the network builder, the lane graph and the city plan without a browser: turn connectors at a crossroads, lane assignment and adjacency, roundabout rings, ramp diverges and merges, invariants and routing. Playwright drives the built site through a debug API: graph invariants, routing between the highway and Main Street, the building-footprint audit, a road-clearance audit that fails if any terrain, tree or prop reaches the pavement, a check that no dead end is left without a destination, city counts, draw-call and triangle budgets, rendered views checked pixel by pixel and kept as screenshots, and the panel against WCAG A and AA.
pieces.title: Verification

pieces.text: A small Fastify server serves the build, in place of the nginx image the site started in, and gives it what the rest of the estate has: a health endpoint and a metrics scrape, JSON logs with the platform's lifecycle events, and a report-only content security policy whose violations it counts. The browser reports what a visit felt like: the Core Web Vitals, and every script error with the source line that threw it, mapped back through the build's source maps. The policy started as strict as the other apps' and opened only for what the scene proved it needs: compiling its WebAssembly decoders, and reading the geometry its models embed.
pieces.title: Serving

automation: Dependabot over npm, the Docker base images and the Actions, grouped weekly with a seven-day cooldown; auto-merge on green for patch and minor, the same policy as the rest of the estate. Base-image majors are not proposed, so the Node runtime only moves on purpose.
CodeQL on every pull request and weekly on main, dependency review, commitlint on the commits and the pull request title, and gitleaks over the full history.

The Playwright suite runs against the production build served by the same server the image runs, on headless Chromium with software WebGL, on a desktop and a mobile viewport, and keeps a screenshot of every camera view as test output so a change to the city can be reviewed by eye as well as by assertion.

stages.text: gitleaks over the staged diff, then format check, lint, typecheck, unit tests with coverage and the build; commitlint on the message; and a pre-push hook that refuses main. The same hooks as the other repositories.
stages.title: Before the commit

stages.text: Quality, then a Docker smoke test of the image, which must answer with the page, its policy header, its health, its metrics and the release it was built with; the Playwright suite — asset pack, lane-graph invariants, routing between the ring highway and Main Street, city counts, a road-clearance audit, performance budgets, pixel samples of every camera view, axe against WCAG A and AA, and the scene loading within its content security policy with its load reaching RUM — a licence gate and npm audit on production dependencies, an SBOM and a Trivy scan of the image, and Semgrep.
stages.title: The pull request

stages.text: release-please derives the version and changelog from the conventional commits on main, and publishes the tag when its pull request is merged.
stages.title: The release

stages.text: On main the image is still built, smoke-tested and left there: nothing ships the scene. The path out of CI is written and in review rather than missing. In this repository a published release builds the web image to ECR, uploads a bundle of the repository to S3 and has SSM bring up a single container on the shared host, by the same path as every other product; in platform-ops, the ingress route, the ECR repository and a deploy role trusted for this repository alone. One container, no database and no secret: the scene is generated in the browser and the server only serves files, a health endpoint, a metrics scrape and the reports the browser sends back, which is why it fits on a host already running twenty-three containers. What is left is not code — the infrastructure has to be applied, the deploy variables set on the repository, and a DNS record pointed at the host — and until something answers behind that name Prometheus is deliberately not told to scrape it, because a job aimed at a container that does not exist would report it down forever.
stages.title: The deploy, written and not yet run

sity.problem: Simulating smart traffic — adaptive signals, rerouting when a road clogs — needs a city that is credible to look at and a road network a program can drive: lanes with direction, turns, ramps and roundabouts, not a picture of asphalt.
sity.tagline: A coastal city built in Three.js as the ground for smart-traffic simulations, with every road already a lane graph.

trading-bot.approach: Latency-sensitive work lives in Rust crates; orchestration and supervision live in TypeScript. The two halves meet at a control plane, with a Next.js operator console on top.
decisions: Backtesting and live execution consume the same strategy crate, so a result that cannot be reproduced offline is a bug rather than a mystery.
The control-plane keeps a URL version because three Rust services call it across a network and deploy separately; the products that ship their client from the same repository do not.

pieces.text: Separate crates for market data, the strategy engine, execution, and research backtesting, so the backtest and the live path can share the same strategy code.
pieces.title: Rust crates

pieces.text: A TypeScript service coordinating the crates and owning the operational API.
pieces.title: Control plane

pieces.text: A Next.js supervision UI built on Tailwind and Radix, sharing the design system with the other products.
pieces.title: Operator console

automation: Dependabot covers npm, Cargo and all five Dockerfiles, so the Rust dependencies get the same weekly attention as the TypeScript ones rather than ageing quietly. Base-image majors are not proposed, so a runtime major only lands on purpose.
Auto-merge on green for patch and minor; majors wait for a person, in both ecosystems.
CodeQL, dependency review and Semgrep on every pull request — the same gate the production repositories use, because the code will need it before it deploys, not after.

The control plane and the operator console both carry the observability code copied in from the platform repository, and a pin beside them records the digest of the kit those copies came from. An edit to a copy fails the pull request without going to the network; the kit having moved on is only reported there and fails a weekly scheduled run instead. The control plane compiles as NodeNext, so its copies carry the file extension on their relative imports, and that difference is declared in the pin with its reason instead of being quietly tolerated.

Local development has two modes over one set of containers, across both languages. `local:dev` runs the control plane under `tsx watch`, the console under `next dev` and the three Rust services under `cargo watch`, all fed by `docker compose watch`. The Rust services share one named volume for the cargo target directory, so the dependency artefacts they have in common are compiled once rather than three times: the first build is long, an incremental one is a few seconds.

stages.text: gitleaks over the staged diff and then the workspace checks, among them the vendored observability code against the kit digest this repository pinned, commitlint on the message, and a pre-push hook that refuses main. The same three hooks as the rest of the estate, so moving between repositories does not mean learning a different set of local rules.
stages.title: Before the commit

stages.text: Two language lanes running side by side. Rust: cargo fmt --check, a lock check that refuses a Cargo.lock disagreeing with the manifests, clippy with warnings denied, and the workspace test suite. TypeScript: format, the vendored kit against its pin, lint, typecheck, build and tests with coverage for the control plane and the operator console. A third lane stands a real PostgreSQL up under Compose and runs the control plane's trade projection against it. Around them, a secret scan, compose manifests rendered against a placeholder env, supply chain and Semgrep.
stages.title: The pull request

stages.text: One version across two languages. release-please bumps both package.json files, the Cargo workspace and both lockfiles from the same conventional commits, so a crate and the console that drives it can never claim different versions of the same release, and no build after a release rewrites a lock.
stages.title: The release

stages.text: There is no deploy workflow on main here either, and the one in review is built so that it cannot start on its own: no release trigger and no push trigger, only a manual dispatch that makes whoever presses it confirm the target host has the memory. The reason is arithmetic rather than caution. Production is one t3.large — two cores and 8 GiB — already running twenty-three containers, and this stack's seven containers measure about 10.6 GiB, of which ClickHouse alone is 5.57 GiB. Sharing that host would mean a t3.2xlarge, roughly four times the compute rate of the one machine the whole estate runs on; a host of its own would still mean a t3.xlarge, with little room left for a large backtest. That is a billing decision rather than a deployment one, so the path is built and left inert, with no production scrape job and no uptime probe behind it: a check pointed at something nobody has started only teaches people to ignore it.
stages.title: A deploy that cannot fire by itself

trading-bot.problem: A strategy that runs unattended needs two very different things: a fast, predictable execution path, and a supervision surface a human can read at a glance. Building both in one language means compromising one of them.
trading-bot.tagline: A trading platform split between a Rust hot path and a TypeScript control plane with an operator console.

0.note: Daily first, then fluent enough to be useful.

intro.lede: Eleven years in production code — developer platforms, build pipelines, and the kind of migrations nobody notices because nothing broke. Currently at Northbound, where deploys went from 51 minutes to 9.
